title: How can technology assist hearing loss? The sound pathway, conductive and sensorineural loss, hearing aids, cochlear implants and bone conduction implants
subtitle: Turn a hearing aid up as far as it goes, and some people still can't make out a word. How can technology assist hearing loss?
subject: Biology
lessonIntent: tracing sound from the outer ear through the eardrum and ossicles (with the pressure concentrated at the small window) to the cochlea, where moving fluid bends hair cells, opening ion channels and triggering signals in the auditory nerve; stating that the cochlea is where vibration becomes a nerve signal, with high pitches near the start of the coil; classifying hearing loss as conductive (outer or middle ear, cochlea working) or sensorineural (hair cells or nerve damaged, usually permanent), with causes of each; explaining how a hearing aid, a cochlear implant and a bone conduction implant each deliver the signal, where each rejoins the pathway, what must still work and which losses each suits; dating the cochlear implant to Graeme Clark's team in Melbourne in 1978; evaluating a cochlear implant (access to sound, not normal hearing; few electrodes; learning; surgery and residual hearing at risk; early implantation for language; consent and Deaf community perspectives); applying this to a fixed stapes and to profound noise-induced loss.

voiceover.text: Turn a hearing aid up as far as it'll go, and some people still can't make out a single word. Volume isn't their problem. Somewhere between the air and the brain, one part has stopped working, and a device only helps if it gets the signal past that part. In 1978, a team in Melbourne found a way past one of those breaks. So how can technology assist hearing loss?

Let's follow the sound. The outer ear funnels sound waves down the ear canal to the eardrum, a thin membrane that vibrates with them. Behind it, in the middle ear, three tiny bones called the ossicles pass that vibration along: malleus, incus, then stapes. The stapes pushes on a small window into the inner ear. That window is much smaller than the eardrum, so the pressure is concentrated, and that's what moves the fluid inside.

In the inner ear, the cochlea is a coiled, fluid-filled tube. As the stapes pushes, waves travel through the fluid and make a membrane inside vibrate. High sounds move it most near the start of the coil, and low sounds further along. Sitting on that membrane are hair cells, the receptors here. When it moves, their tiny hairs bend, ion channels open, and the cell triggers signals in the auditory nerve, which carries them to the brain. So the cochlea is where vibration becomes a nerve signal.

That gives two main kinds of hearing loss. In conductive loss, sound can't get through the outer or middle ear. The canal might be blocked, fluid might fill the middle ear after an infection, the eardrum might be torn, or the stapes might be stuck. The cochlea still works. In sensorineural loss, the hair cells or the auditory nerve are damaged, by loud noise, ageing, genes or some infections. Human hair cells don't grow back, so this loss is usually permanent.

Now match a device to the break. A hearing aid sits behind or in the ear. A microphone picks up sound, an amplifier makes it louder, mostly at the pitches the person hears worst, and a tiny speaker sends it down the canal. That louder sound still travels the normal path, so it needs some hair cells that still work. It can help when enough usable hearing remains. But if most hair cells are gone, louder sound has nothing left to stimulate.

A cochlear implant skips the hair cells. A processor behind the ear turns sound into a coded electrical signal. A coil sends it through the skin, by radio, to a receiver under the skin. The receiver sends pulses down a thin array of electrodes threaded along the cochlea. Each electrode stimulates the nerve fibres at its position, so electrodes near the start of the coil signal high pitches. The hair cells are bypassed, but the auditory nerve must still work.

This is an Australian story. In 1978, Graeme Clark and his team at the University of Melbourne implanted their multi-channel cochlear implant in their first patient, and that work grew into implants now used around the world. But an implant doesn't restore normal hearing. About twelve to twenty-two electrical channels replace the richer coding of about three and a half thousand inner hair cells, so the sound is coarser. The brain learns to use it over months, and music is often harder than speech. It also needs surgery, which can damage hearing left in that ear.

The third device uses a route you already use. You hear your own voice partly through the bones of your skull. A bone conduction implant works that way. A small titanium screw is fixed into the skull bone behind the ear, and the bone grows onto it. A sound processor attached to it turns sound into vibration, which travels through the skull to the cochlea. It skips the outer and middle ear, so it suits conductive or mixed loss. It can also help deafness in one ear, by sending sound across to the working cochlea. But it needs a working cochlea.

So the three devices aren't ranked, they're matched. A hearing aid makes sound louder, so enough of the pathway must still work. A bone conduction implant skips the outer and middle ear, so the cochlea must work. A cochlear implant skips the hair cells, so the nerve must work. For a baby born deaf, implanting early gives spoken language the best start, but the child can't consent. Many Deaf people use Auslan, Australian Sign Language, and see deafness as a culture and community, so families weigh both.

Two exam questions. First. A forty-five-year-old has otosclerosis: bone growth has fixed the stapes, so it can't vibrate. Tests show the cochlea and auditory nerve work normally. Identify the type of hearing loss. Then explain why a bone conduction implant could help, and why a cochlear implant would not be suitable. Pause here to answer.

It's conductive loss: the stuck stapes stops vibration reaching the cochlea, which still works, and so does the nerve. A bone conduction implant sends vibration through the skull straight to that cochlea, skipping the stapes. A cochlear implant would bypass healthy hair cells, and surgery could damage their natural hearing. The classic mistake is choosing the cochlear implant because it's the most advanced.

Second. A sixty-year-old worked for decades in loud factories and now has profound sensorineural loss in both ears. Powerful hearing aids gave almost no benefit, and tests show both auditory nerves work. Evaluate a cochlear implant for this person. Pause here to answer.

Noise has destroyed most of the hair cells, so louder sound has little left to stimulate. An implant bypasses them and stimulates the working nerves directly, giving access to sound. But it won't be normal hearing: few electrodes, months of learning, and surgery that risks any hearing left. On balance, it's a strong choice here. The classic mistake is writing that the implant restores normal hearing.

So for any hearing technology question, follow the sound to the break. Ask what still works, then choose the device that delivers the signal just past the broken part. Next, the same idea for the eye: how technology can assist visual disorders.
